chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
title: Contact between black and white musicians and integration
summary: Contact between the races began to improve in the late Twenties; the real change in the music came around 1935-36 with Dizzy and Parker, and integrated bands today work better.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there much contact between musicians?
Not as much as there should have been. You mean between the two races?
It wasn't as much as it should have been. It started getting better. In the late Twenties, it started to get a little better.
So would guys sometimes... When bands would run into each other in the same town, would you hang out together and listen to each other?
There wasn't too much of that. Until the late Twenties, around '28, that things started getting a little better.
Could that have been also much of a change in the music, too? Like...

There wasn't too much change in the music. The change in the music came around...oh, I'd say around '35 or '36, getting close to the war-time. Then Dizzy came along, Charlie Parker and all... They just had like Swing bands, you know... Swing bands...
But what I meant in this particular case was specifically if the White musicians started listening more to Black musicians, and the music became closer together.
Yeah, it did. It did. And now bands are integrated, and that's great for them. They sound better and they work better. Better relations in every way, you know.
